title: Black Book
full_review:
With its opening scenes in a 1950s Israeli kibbutz, and its principal action set in 1944 Nazi-occupied Holland, "Black Book" (Sony Classics) looks on paper to be "Basic Instinct" and "Showgirls" director Paul Verhoeven's bid for a serious-minded film like "Schindler's List."

Well, not exactly. Though the movie doesn't trivialize its weighty themes of wartime ambivalence and betrayal, and the line between villain and hero is blurred in some intriguing ways, this is primarily a glossy and well-acted World War II spy saga of the kind they don't make anymore.

The Jewish Rachel Stein, played by a compelling Carice van Houten, is a cabaret singer hiding out with a Christian family headed by a stern patriarch who autocratically demands she memorize her New Testament. After the house is bombed, she arranges to flee the country with her family.

Just prior to making the journey, she goes to the office of an elderly family lawyer (Dolf de Vries) to withdraw some of her money and jewelry, and he writes her name in his little black book, which gives the film its title and figures in the action later on.

In any case, as the boat carries them to freedom, the family is ambushed and all but she are slaughtered.

The bereft Rachel decides to join the Dutch Resistance run by Gerben Kuipers (Derek de Lint). After going on a gun-smuggling mission, her next assignment is to seduce and spy on Ludwig Muntze (Sebastian Koch, charismatic star of this year's German Oscar winner, "The Lives of Others"), the head of the Gestapo with whom she has already had a chance encounter on a train.
Muntze hires her to be his assistant, which gives her an inside track at Gestapo headquarters. There, she befriends Ronnie (Halina Reijn), an amoral gal (with a proverbial heart of gold) involved with a lecherous Nazi.

Rachel and Muntze genuinely fall in love, even after he learns Rachel is Jewish, and Muntze proves to be a man of conscience who eventually tries to negotiate the release of Dutch prisoners, one of whom is Kuipers' beloved son.

The action-packed plot includes many twists, and characters who turn out to be not what they first appear.

For all the film's seeming improbability, Verhoeven and co-scriptwriter Gerard Soeteman say it is based on "true events" and "real people." Maybe so, but "Black Book" registers mainly as escapist entertainment.

Verhoeven's old-style Hollywood production unfortunately comes with a good deal of present-day permissiveness. Though the sex per se is not too graphic, there is some full-frontal nudity, along with several scenes of generalized decadence. And there is strong wartime violence. But on both scores, Verhoeven shows at least more restraint than in his prior films.

Still, the frankness of some of the material -- arguably not all dramatically valid -- and a troubling revenge plot involving two of the principals, will preclude viewing for many Catholics, and should thus be approached with caution.

In Dutch, German, English and Hebrew, with subtitles.

The film contains strong rough and crude language and profanity, sexual encounters, full male and female nudity, innuendo, wartime violence including shootings and beatings, and vigilante justice. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
